cells.tense: Right now the ending is here and you are standing in it without flinching.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: This week, when you give something — an hour, a hand, a meal — let something come back, and don't hand it away at the door.
cells.core: You can tell the difference between something finished and something merely hard, and you act on it. What ends, ends because it is done, not because it failed, and you don't drag the old shape behind you into what comes next. People feel it in the way you care — steady, unhurried, no grip. The give and take in that care tends to run one direction more than you'd choose. Checking on what you tend, taking a hand when it's offered, letting a meal be cooked for you — small returns. That's not keeping score. It's what keeps the care from running dry. Try it once this week and see what shifts.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what's finished, and you let it finish.
cells.verb: ending what has finished so what is next can begin
cells.place: where what is growing is tended without being forced

cells.tense: You will be braced for the next rupture before the present one has even settled.
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Stay with whoever is carrying something heavy, in it, for a while, and fix nothing.
cells.core: You can see the ending coming, and you can see it everywhere. Something gets clear enough to be finished and you finish it before it's lived, and the release seems like gain while it lasts. There is real ending in you, and it has started arriving ahead of what it belongs to. The way through starts with whoever is across from you. The mess and the person need company, not a rescue committee. Sit with them in it a while; don't tidy it, don't hand them a cleaner version. Stay in your own seat while you do. If they ask what you see, then you can say it.
cells.sheetLine: The ending is arriving before the thing it belongs to has finished.

cells.tense: You were standing at that door long after it had already closed behind you.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Follow a pull you already feel — somewhere, someone, some direction — and go a little way toward it.
cells.core: You keep something alive past the point where it can grow. There's loyalty in that — to a person, a role, a version of things — and it's holding you at an address you've already left. Not because you can't end things. Because ending feels like the wrong answer, so you keep watering what's already gone. What moves you out isn't a reckoning. It's motion in whatever direction something in you is already leaning. The pull is the direction; it doesn't have to be large or reasoned. Take a step before it's tidy, before the last piece is in place. The ending happens on the way, not before it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep watering something that's already finished growing.

cells.tense: Something in you is finishing right now and you have not yet put it into words.
cells.act: put a date, a place, a container on it
cells.ask: Give what you're carrying a container — a time, a room, a place it lives.
cells.core: You are good at caring for what's growing — steady, patient, no forcing. And you haven't looked at what's ending, or that anything is. The ending is real and unnamed, and the care is aimed elsewhere. What brings it into view is a small structure. Not a reckoning — one container. A time on the calendar, one room for the thing, one hour set aside for what's actually going on in you. The mess doesn't have to be solved; it has to be given walls. Put it somewhere you'll see it. That's not making a decision. That's making the decision visible when it's ready.
cells.sheetLine: The ending is happening and you haven't looked at it yet.

attempts.check: The draft's risk is claiming the person is actually ending something or clinging to something — the record only shows the capacity's position, not events; a reader could rightly say 'nothing is dying, I just have a full week.' The asks survive being wrong because each is one small act doable without the read being true — they teach calibration, contact, one step, one container regardless. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line announcing what must end; I've kept the mechanism and left the person's history alone.
